<!-- read as: markdown -->
The U.S. experience shows quite a range—from tariffs that produced almost no detectable retail-price increase to cases where consumer prices rose by nearly the full economic effect of the tariff. A key distinction is where in the supply chain you measure the price.

| Episode | Observed price behavior | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Washing machines, 2012 & 2016 antidumping duties | Little or no consumer-price increase | Tariffs applied to particular countries; manufacturers shifted production to other countries |
| Washing machines, 2018 safeguard tariff | Washer prices rose about 12%; untariffed dryers rose similarly | Tariff applied broadly across source countries, making trade diversion harder; firms also repriced complementary goods |
| China tariffs, 2018–19, broad retail sample | Importers paid nearly the full tariff, but retail prices increased much less in many categories | Retailers/wholesalers absorbed some cost by reducing margins |
| Steel/aluminum tariffs, 2018–21 | U.S. steel prices +2.4%, aluminum +1.6%; downstream products only about +0.2% on average | Tariff cost was diluted because metal is only one input into finished products |
| Chinese tire safeguard, 2009 | Substantial increase in tire costs to consumers | Alternative suppliers and domestic producers also charged more |
| 2025 tariffs, recent research | Estimated about 26% of the tariff increase passed through to consumer prices | Direct import-price increases plus slower indirect effects through inputs and reduced competition |

One particularly revealing comparison: washing machines

The washing-machine episodes are unusually good natural experiments.

In 2012, the U.S. imposed antidumping duties on Korean and Mexican production, and in 2016 on Chinese production. Manufacturers responded by moving production—for example, from China to Vietnam and Thailand. The study finds these tariffs were:

“accompanied by downward or minor price movements along with production relocation”

TopCat

So even though particular imports became expensive, the market price didn't rise much because firms could change the country of origin.

The 2018 safeguard tariff was quite different: it covered washing machines from nearly everywhere. That escape route largely disappeared. The same researchers found:

“the price of washers increased nearly 12 percent”

and, remarkably, dryers—which weren't tariffed—rose by about the same amount. TopCat+1

The dryer result illustrates another mechanism: retailers and manufacturers don't necessarily price each item according to its individual marginal cost. Washers and dryers are commonly sold as matched pairs, so firms spread the increased cost over both products.

The 2018 China tariffs: border prices versus store prices

This is perhaps the most important distinction.

Studies of the 2018–19 tariffs found that Chinese exporters generally didn't cut their pre-tariff prices enough to offset the tariff. The tariff therefore showed up almost completely in what American importers paid.

Cavallo, Gopinath, Neiman and Tang found:

“the tariffs were almost fully passed through to total prices paid by importers”

But at the retail level:

“the tariffs’ impact on retail prices is more mixed.”

National Bureau of Economic Research

That isn't contradictory. Suppose something previously costs:

• Chinese exporter: $70
• wholesale/importer costs: $10
• retailer margin: $20
• consumer price: $100

A 25% tariff on the $70 import is $17.50. The importer may really pay essentially all $17.50, but the retail chain could respond with something like:

• importer cost: +$17.50
• wholesale/retail margins: −$10
• retail price: +$7.50

So 100% tariff pass-through at customs can coexist with much lower consumer-price pass-through.

The researchers found evidence consistent with exactly that:

“the difference between affected and unaffected products is generally quite modest, suggesting that retail margins have fallen.”

National Bureau of Economic Research

Steel and aluminum: large upstream effect, small finished-goods effect

The USITC's retrospective analysis of the 2018 Section 232 and Section 301 tariffs found very high pass-through at the border:

“prices increased by about 1 percent for each 1 percent increase in the tariffs”

for imports subject to these tariffs. USITC

But that didn't mean a 25% steel tariff raised cars or machinery prices by 25%. The USITC estimated that the Section 232 tariffs caused:

• steel prices: +2.4%
• aluminum prices: +1.6%
• prices in downstream industries using those metals: +0.2% on average

USITC

The dilution makes sense. If steel accounts for 5% of the cost of some finished product and steel gets 3% more expensive, the direct cost effect is only roughly 0.15% of the finished product's price.

Another mechanism: domestic producers can raise prices too

Tariffs don't just affect imported products. If an imported competitor becomes more expensive, a domestic producer may also have room to charge more.

This showed up clearly with washing machines: domestic brands raised their prices even though their machines weren't themselves paying the import tariff. American Economic Association

Recent research on the 2025 tariffs explicitly decomposes this effect. Amiti, Heise and Weinstein estimate that about 26% of the tariff increase appeared in consumer prices, with roughly two-thirds coming directly through imported goods and the rest indirectly through input costs and domestic firms' markups. They write:

“tariffs raise the prices of goods made at home, not just the imports they tax”

National Bureau of Economic Research

They also find that the indirect effects take longer—roughly 9–12 months—to work through supply chains. National Bureau of Economic Research

What determines whether prices rise?

The main variables are therefore:

1. How easy it is to switch suppliers.
A tariff on China alone may cause sourcing to move to Vietnam. A tariff on imports from nearly everywhere doesn't leave that option.
2. Whether foreign exporters cut their prices.
Economically, this depends on supply/demand elasticities and bargaining power. In the 2018 U.S. tariffs, the evidence generally finds surprisingly little reduction in exporters' pre-tariff prices.
3. Retailer/importer margins.
Firms can temporarily accept lower profits rather than immediately raising sticker prices.
4. Domestic competition.
If imports become less competitive, domestic manufacturers may raise prices too. Thus consumer prices can rise even for non-tariffed domestic goods.
5. How large the tariffed input is relative to the final product.
A 25% tariff on a component making up 2% of a product's cost has a much smaller direct effect than a 25% tariff on the finished product.
6. Pricing relationships among products.
The washer/dryer example shows that firms may spread the tariff cost across complementary goods.
7. Inventories and contracts.
Existing inventory bought before the tariff can postpone price increases; long-term supplier contracts can do the same.
8. Time horizon.
Immediate effects may appear primarily at customs. Months later, sourcing changes, input costs, domestic markups, and investment responses start appearing.
9. Demand conditions.
A retailer facing weak demand may find it difficult to raise prices and instead accept lower margins. With strong demand, passing costs on is easier.

This also explains an apparent puzzle in tariff studies: “Who pays the tariff?” doesn't have a single answer unless you specify the stage and time horizon. For the 2018 tariffs, there's strong evidence that American importers initially bore almost the entire statutory cost. How much eventually reached consumers depended substantially on the particular industry and firms' responses. National Bureau of Economic Research+1
